records.text: Generative models produce objects of high dimensionality and complex structure — images, text, music, video.
In deep learning, the first major divide lies between explicit density models and implicit density models.
An explicit density model provides a formula for $p(x)$, the probability density of the data.
Even though the true distribution of, for example, cat photos in a multi-million-dimensional pixel space is impossibly complicated, an explicit approximation can be built.
Tractable density models can write down $p(x)$ as a closed-form product of conditional distributions.

The classic example of a tractable density model is an autoregressive model, which decomposes $p(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) = p(x_1) p(x_2 \mid x_1) p(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2) \cdots p(x_n \mid x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$.
The autoregressive decomposition identity is always true.

To make the decomposition useful, simplifying assumptions are introduced, such as a Markov chain, an RNN with a hidden state, or a Transformer that conditions each next token on the preceding context.
All large language models (LLMs) are autoregressive models that generate text one token at a time.
Pixel-wise autoregressive models for images, such as PixelCNN, exist.
Generating a million pixels a million times with pixel-wise autoregressive models is prohibitively slow.
In approximate density models, instead of forcing $p(x)$ itself to be tractable, $p(x)$ is approximated with a simpler distribution $q(x)$ that is easy to handle.
The most important family of approximate density models are Variational Autoencoders (VAEs).
VAEs use variational inference to build a learnable lower bound on the log-likelihood.
VAEs are a cornerstone of generative modelling.
Diffusion models typically operate in the latent space of a VAE.
Flow-based models are an alternative approach that composes many simple, invertible transformations so that the density $p(x)$ can be computed by the change-of-variables formula.
Flow-based models belong to explicit density models.
Flow-based models are not covered in this lecture.
An implicit density model never provides a formula for $p(x)$.
An implicit density model is just a sampler: you feed in random noise and get out a sample $\hat{x}$ that should look like it came from the data distribution.
There is no way to read off a density from a trained implicit density network; you can only draw from it.
The main example of implicit density models is Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).
A generator $G$ maps a random noise vector $z$ drawn from $p_z(z)$, such as a standard Gaussian, to an output $\hat{x}$ that should resemble a real image.
In the generator's training, there is no paired supervision; there is no mapping that specifies which $z$ should produce which particular $x$.
There is no obvious loss function that directly evaluates the quality of a generated image.
The central challenge of generative adversarial networks is how to score the generator's output.
The GAN solution is to learn the loss function itself.

A second network, the discriminator $D$, is introduced; its job is binary classification: it determines whether an image came from the real data distribution $p_{\text{data}}$ (output 1) or from the generator $p_g$ (output 0).
The generator and discriminator have opposing objectives: $D$ wants to tell real from fake, and $G$ wants to fool $D$.
This is called adversarial training.
The generator is defined as $G(z; \theta_g): Z \to X$ and the discriminator as $D(x; \theta_d): X \to [0,1]$.
The discriminator maximizes the log-likelihood of correct classification given by $L_D = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g(x)}[\log(1 - D(x))]$.
The generator wants to minimize the same quantity, trying to push $D(G(z))$ towards 1, i.e., fool the discriminator.
The combined objective is the minimax game $\min_G \max_D V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$.
This is not ordinary optimisation; it is a zero-sum game where two players are competing.
In principle, finding an equilibrium in a zero-sum game is much harder than a simple minimisation.
However, the structure of the GAN problem makes finding an equilibrium feasible.
For a fixed generator, the optimal discriminator is given by $D^*_G(x) = \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x)}$.
Plugging the optimal discriminator into the value function yields the Jensen–Shannon divergence between $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$.

The Jensen–Shannon divergence is defined as $\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\text{data}} \| p_g) = \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\text{data}} \;\middle\|\; \frac{p_{\text{data}}+p_g}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_g \;\middle\|\; \frac{p_{\text{data}}+p_g}{2}\right)$.
At the global minimum of the GAN game, the generator's distribution equals the data distribution: $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$.
The theoretical generator loss $\mathbb{E}_z[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$ is very poor for training the generator in practice.
The problem is sigmoid-saturated cross-entropy.
When the discriminator becomes good at separating real from fake, it gives confident predictions with $D(G(z)) \approx 0$.
In that case, the gradient of $\log(1-D)$ saturates and nearly vanishes.
Then backpropagation through $D$ provides almost no signal to $G$, exactly when the generator needs to improve the most.
The practical fix is to use a non-saturating loss for the generator: minimize $-\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log D(G(z))]$.
This means maximizing the probability that the discriminator makes a mistake, rather than minimizing the probability of its correct answer.
This non-saturating loss keeps the gradient alive when the discriminator is strong.
Training of GANs proceeds in alternation, much like an EM algorithm.
Step 1: Fix $G$ and update $D$ by improving the binary cross-entropy on mini-batches of real data and generated data.
Step 2: Fix $D$ and update $G$ using the non-saturating loss.
In practice, the discriminator is often updated more frequently, or the updates are carefully balanced to avoid one network overpowering the other too quickly.
The original GAN (2014) produced reasonable digits on MNIST but struggled with diverse, natural images.
A major advance was Deep Convolutional GANs (DCGANs).
DCGANs replaced fully-connected layers with convolutional/deconvolutional architectures.
DCGANs used strided convolutions instead of pooling.
DCGANs added batch normalization everywhere.
DCGANs were trained with the Adam optimizer.
After only a few epochs on a dataset such as LSUN bedrooms, DCGAN could produce recognizable images of size 64×64 or 128×128.
These DCGAN results were state-of-the-art a decade ago.
These results already hinted at the latent space structure.
To tell if a generator has learned a meaningful mapping and not just memorized training examples, a visual test is used.
The discriminator cannot answer whether the generator has learned a meaningful mapping.
The discriminator's inability to distinguish real from generated merely indicates it is not powerful enough or not well trained.
A widely used visual test is a linear walk in the latent space.
The generator can be thought of as a map from a simple latent distribution $Z$, such as a standard Gaussian, to a point $X$ on the complicated manifold of real images.
To generate new images, we need to be able to sample a random $z$ and land reliably on the real image manifold.
In a linear walk, two latent vectors $z_1$ and $z_2$ that both produce plausible images are interpolated linearly.
Every intermediate point of the linear interpolation should also produce a plausible image.
If the images blur or morph unrealistically during interpolation, the manifold is not well flattened.
Good DCGANs show smooth, realistic transitions during linear walks in latent space.
Smooth latent walks confirm that the latent space is well-behaved and that sampling from the prior yields reasonable outputs.
Early GANs, including DCGAN, exhibited characteristic failures stemming from the local receptive fields of convolution.
The generator builds an image part by part with limited global context.
One failure mode is counting problems, such as three-headed dogs or multiple eyes.
Counting problems occur because the model does not know how many of a repeated feature to produce, since it only sees a small neighborhood.
Another failure mode is perspective inconsistencies, where different halves of an object may be rendered from different viewpoints.
Perspective inconsistencies occur because the generator has no global 3D understanding.
These mistakes are easy for humans to spot.
These mistakes reflect the difficulty of enforcing global coherence with purely local operations.
A crucial idea for scaling up resolution in GANs is to not generate the whole image at once.
Progressive Growing GAN (ProGAN) trains a GAN in stages.
ProGAN starts from $4 \times 4$ pixels and progressively adds layers that quadruple the resolution up to $1024 \times 1024$.
At each stage, new convolutional layers are added smoothly to both the generator and the discriminator.
This approach allows the model to first learn large-scale structure and then refine it.
Training time is saved because the early stages see many more lower-resolution images.
After about two weeks of training on powerful hardware, ProGAN produced the first high-resolution, photo-realistic human faces.
These faces are known from the website "ThisPersonDoesNotExist".
At the time, ProGAN incorporated improved loss functions.
One improved loss function was the Least Squares GAN (LSGAN).
LSGAN replaces the sigmoid cross-entropy with a squared-deviation target.
The LSGAN discriminator loss is $\min_D \frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{\text{data}}}[(D(x)-b)^2] + \frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_z}[(D(G(z))-a)^2]$.
The LSGAN generator loss is $\min_G \frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_z}[(D(G(z))-c)^2]$.
Typical choices for LSGAN are $a=0$, $b=c=1$.
Because the LSGAN loss penalizes overshooting, nothing explodes to infinity, and gradients remain useful.

The deeper reason why standard divergences cause trouble in generative modeling is that $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$ are concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds inside the high-dimensional pixel space.
The support of a realistic cat photo set is a tiny, intricate surface in $\mathbb{R}^{3\mathrm{M}}$.
The generator maps a low-dimensional noise vector to an image, so its distribution $p_g$ also lies on some low-dimensional manifold.
In the beginning of training, these two manifolds almost surely do not intersect; their overlap has measure zero.

In the Kullback-Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}} \| p_g) = \int p_{\text{data}}(x) \log \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_g(x)}\,dx$, where $p_{\text{data}}(x) > 0$, we typically have $p_g(x) = 0$.
Thus the logarithm becomes infinite, making the KL divergence undefined or infinite.
This yields no useful gradient to move $p_g$ towards $p_{\text{data}}$.
Classical machine learning avoids this problem by adding Gaussian noise to the model, smoothing its support everywhere.
But in implicit generative models, we cannot remove that noise during generation, because adding noise blurs the images and defeats the purpose.
The Earth Mover distance (Wasserstein-1) provides a solution to the manifold mismatch problem.
Intuitively, think of the two probability distributions as piles of earth of total volume 1.
The Wasserstein distance is the minimum amount of work needed to turn one pile into the other, where work is approximately mass times distance moved.

Formally, $W(p_{\text{data}}, p_g) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(p_{\text{data}}, p_g)} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \gamma}[\|x - y\|]$, where $\Pi(p_{\text{data}}, p_g)$ is the set of joint distributions whose marginals are $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$.
Crucially, the Wasserstein distance remains continuous and provides meaningful gradients even when the supports of the distributions are disjoint.
Moving a distribution a little bit closer always reduces the Earth Mover distance, whereas the KL divergence would still be infinite.
Computing the infimum over joint distributions in the Wasserstein distance seems intractable.

The Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality transforms the Wasserstein distance into a supremum over 1-Lipschitz functions: $W(p_{\text{data}}, p_g) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \le 1} (\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g}[f(x)])$.
We can parametrize $f$ with a neural network $f_w$, called the critic, because it no longer does binary classification.
Originally, the Lipschitz constraint was enforced by weight clipping to a small range.
In WGAN training, for a fixed generator, the critic is trained to maximize the difference of expectations, approximating the Wasserstein distance.
For a fixed critic, the generator's gradient is computed as $-\mathbb{E}_{z}[\nabla_\theta f_w(G_\theta(z))]$, and the generator is updated.
The WGAN loss correlates much better with image quality than the standard GAN loss.
The WGAN critic can be trained to convergence, unlike the discriminator in a standard GAN.
Weight clipping can cause the critic to learn over-simplified functions and may lead to exploding or vanishing gradients.
Improved WGAN (WGAN-GP) replaces weight clipping with a soft gradient penalty.

The gradient penalty term is $\lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x} \sim P_{\hat{x}}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]$, where $\hat{x}$ is sampled uniformly along straight lines between real and generated samples.
This gradient penalty encourages the critic's gradient norm to stay close to 1 everywhere.
This enforces the Lipschitz condition in a gentler way and yields more stable training.
Further improvements in GANs addressed the locality of convolutions and scaled up the models.
Self‑Attention GAN (SAGAN) adds a Transformer‑like self‑attention mechanism over image features.
This self‑attention mechanism lets the generator capture long‑range dependencies.
The attention maps of SAGAN show that the network looks far across the image when synthesising fine details.
BigGAN combined self‑attention with very large architectures and careful regularisation.
BigGAN improved the Inception score threefold.
BigGAN produced high‑fidelity interpolations, such as smoothly morphing a bird into a dog with plausible intermediate hybrids.
Evaluating image quality itself is non‑trivial.
The Inception score is a commonly used metric.
To compute the Inception score, one takes a generated image $x$ and runs a pre‑trained Inception classifier to get $p(y \mid x)$.
The Inception score is defined as $\mathrm{IS} = \exp\!\Bigl( \mathbb{E}_x \,\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p(y \mid x) \,\|\, p(y)\bigr) \Bigr)$.
In the Inception score formula, $p(y)$ is defined as $p(y) = \int p(y \mid G(z))\, dz$.

The Inception score rewards images that are confidently classified as a particular class (low entropy in $p(y \mid x)$) while the generated set as a whole is diverse across classes (high entropy in $p(y)$).
A natural way to obtain a loss function for generation is to train an autoencoder.
In an autoencoder, an encoder maps an image $x$ to a latent code $z$.
In an autoencoder, a decoder maps $z$ back to a reconstruction $\hat{x}$.
Training an autoencoder minimises $\|x - \hat{x}\|^2$.
After training an autoencoder, the decoder alone can function as a generator by feeding it a latent code $z$ to get an image.
The aggregated posterior distribution of latent codes produced by the autoencoder's encoder on real data is complicated and not easy to sample from.
Simply drawing $z$ from a standard Gaussian and feeding it to the autoencoder's decoder will almost certainly miss the correct manifold, producing garbage.
An Adversarial Autoencoder (AAE) solves the sampling problem by adding a discriminator in the latent space.
In an AAE, the discriminator learns to distinguish between latent codes from the encoder (from real data) and samples from a simple prior (e.g., a standard Gaussian).
In an AAE, the encoder is simultaneously trained to fool the discriminator, pushing its output distribution to match the prior.
Once an AAE is trained, sampling $z$ from the Gaussian and passing it through the decoder yields plausible images.
AAEs can be extended to conditional generation by providing a label to the encoder and decoder.
AAEs can be extended to semi‑supervised learning.
VAEs offer a cleaner probabilistic regularisation compared to AAEs.
AAEs are a direct, adversarial alternative to VAEs.
AAEs still see use.
In Conditional GANs, the generator receives both a noise vector and a conditioning input (e.g., a class label, a low‑resolution image, or an age descriptor).
Conditional GANs enable tasks such as face ageing and super‑resolution (e.g., ESRGAN).
Stacked GANs (SGAN) are a chain of GANs where later stages condition on the output of earlier ones, progressively refining the representation through a hierarchy.
GANs were the state‑of‑the‑art for unconditional image generation until around 2020.
GANs remain strong in specific niches, such as super‑resolution, style transfer, and any domain where an explicit density is not needed.
For text‑to‑image generation and large‑scale prompted image synthesis, diffusion models have taken over.
The principle of adversarial training is still embedded in many modern pipelines.
The next lecture will introduce diffusion models and show how they connect to the ideas discussed today.
